title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 7
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain extended its opening hours to include Sunday evenings and reports that its total weekly prescriptions dispensed have not increased. The chain concludes that there is no demand for Sunday evening opening.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some staff dislike working on Sundays.
B. Sunday evening prescriptions are substantial, and have been drawn almost entirely from customers who previously queued on Monday mornings.
C. The chain advertised the new hours only in its shop windows.
D. Competing pharmacies remain closed on Sundays.
E. Prescription volumes vary seasonally.
questions.explanation: Redistribution within the week is compatible with real demand for the new slot; the total is simply the wrong measure of it. C would explain low uptake, but the passage reports uptake has occurred.

questions.prompt: An agricultural adviser notes that fields receiving the heaviest applications of nitrogen fertiliser in the Coleby district produce the highest yields, and recommends that farmers with lower yields increase their applications.
questions.question: The recommendation depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Nitrogen fertiliser has fallen in price.
B. All farmers in the district measure their yields in the same way.
C. The lower-yielding fields are not limited by some other factor, such as drainage or soil depth, that additional nitrogen would not remedy.
D. Nitrogen is the only fertiliser applied in the district.
E. The highest-yielding fields have the same crop rotation as the others.
questions.explanation: If a different constraint binds, more nitrogen adds cost without yield — and the heaviest applications may be going to the best land precisely because it responds. C and D are tidiness conditions rather than requirements of the inference.

questions.prompt: A gym chain replaced its monthly membership with an annual contract paid in advance, and reports that members on annual contracts attend more often than monthly members did.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this result without supposing that annual contracts increase motivation?
options: A. Members who expected to attend rarely chose not to commit for a year, so the annual group contains a larger share of frequent attenders.
B. Annual contracts are slightly cheaper per month.
C. The chain refurbished several gyms in the same period.
D. Attendance is recorded electronically.
E. Some members transfer between branches.
questions.explanation: Composition rather than behaviour: the contract selected the attenders instead of creating them. C offers a rival cause but one that would raise attendance genuinely, which is what the question asks to avoid.

questions.prompt: A lender found that loan applicants who complete the application form in a single sitting default less often than those who return to it over several days. It plans to use completion in a single sitting as a factor in deciding whom to lend to.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the plan?
options: A. Some applicants complete the form on a mobile telephone.
B. The lender's default rate is lower than the industry average.
C. The form takes about twenty minutes to complete.
D. Once applicants learn that uninterrupted completion improves their chances, the behaviour will no longer distinguish the careful from the rest.
E. Applicants are not told how their applications are assessed.
questions.explanation: A predictor that people can costlessly imitate stops predicting once it is used — the standard failure of behavioural proxies in credit scoring. E would delay that outcome, not prevent it.

questions.prompt: Every classroom in the Fenwick school that was fitted with an air filter last year also had its windows replaced. No classroom with replaced windows recorded a temperature complaint this winter. Some classrooms in the school recorded temperature complaints this winter.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Air filters prevent temperature complaints.
B. Every classroom with an air filter is warmer than those without.
C. No classroom in the school recorded a temperature complaint.
D. Most classrooms had their windows replaced.
E. Some classrooms were not fitted with an air filter last year.
questions.explanation: Complaints exist; a filtered classroom has replaced windows and so no complaint, therefore the complaining classrooms have no filter. A asserts causation the statements do not support, and D contradicts a premise.

questions.prompt: A coastal town is considering a levy on overnight visitors to fund improvements to its seafront, on the grounds that visitors impose costs on local services and that the improvements will attract more visitors.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the proposal?
options: A. Whether residents support the improvements
B. Whether visitors would continue to come in similar numbers with the levy in place
C. How the levy would be collected
D. Whether neighbouring towns have seafront improvements
E. How long the improvements would take to complete
questions.explanation: The proposal is self-undermining if the levy deters the visitors whose payments fund it and whose numbers it aims to increase. B and C matter to implementation, not to whether the scheme achieves its aim.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer reports that apprentices trained in its own workshops are more productive after three years than employees hired with equivalent external qualifications, and concludes that its apprenticeship is a better form of training.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that productivity can be measured accurately
B. ignores the cost of running an apprenticeship
C. compares workers of different ages
D. overlooks that apprentices who proved unsuitable left during the three years, while external hires were measured from their first day
E. relies on the manufacturer's own records
questions.explanation: Survivorship: the apprentice group has been filtered by three years of attrition, so the comparison is between a selected group and an unselected one. C is a fair question about value, not about the inference.

questions.prompt: A supermarket reduced the weight of packaging on its own-brand products by 20 per cent and announced that this had cut the environmental impact of its packaging by a fifth.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the supermarket's announcement?
options: A. Customers have not noticed the change.
B. The lighter packaging costs less to produce.
C. A quarter of the lightened products now arrive damaged and are discarded, and the discarded goods carry a far larger footprint than the packaging saved.
D. Other supermarkets have made similar reductions.
E. Packaging is only part of a product's total footprint.
questions.explanation: Damage transfers the impact rather than removing it, and the transferred quantity is larger. E is true but generic; it does not challenge the specific claim about packaging.

questions.prompt: Wildlife crossings built over a motorway have been used by deer, and the number of deer-vehicle collisions on that stretch has fallen. A transport department concludes that the crossings caused the reduction.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The crossings were expensive to construct.
B. Deer are most active at dawn and dusk.
C. Motorists report seeing fewer deer near the road.
D. The crossings are planted with vegetation.
E. Collisions on comparable stretches of the same motorway, where no crossings were built, did not change over the same period.
questions.explanation: Unchanged collisions on comparable stretches removes general explanations such as traffic volume or deer numbers. D is consistent with the conclusion but also with deer simply having declined.

questions.prompt: A microfinance organisation reports that borrowers who received loans have higher household incomes two years later than applicants who were rejected, and presents this as evidence that its loans raise incomes.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the presentation?
options: A. Applicants are rejected precisely when the organisation judges their businesses least likely to succeed.
B. Some borrowers repay early.
C. The loans carry interest at market rates.
D. Household income is measured by survey.
E. The organisation operates in several districts.
questions.explanation: The comparison group was selected for expected failure, so the two groups differed before any loan was made. D raises measurement noise but not systematic bias between groups.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to classify food delivery couriers as employees argue that couriers currently bear costs — vehicle maintenance, insurance, waiting time — that employers would otherwise pay. Opponents reply that many couriers say they value the freedom to choose their hours.
questions.question: The opponents' reply is weakest in that it
options: A. denies that couriers bear any costs
B. relies on the testimony of couriers
C. treats the freedom to choose hours and employee status as though they could not coexist
D. assumes that couriers understand their contracts
E. addresses only couriers who work part-time
questions.explanation: Employment status and flexible scheduling are separable; the reply answers a claim about who bears costs with a claim about hours, as if one excluded the other.

questions.passageTitle: Selling the Same Thing at Different Prices
questions.passageText:
A firm that could charge each customer exactly what that customer was willing to pay would capture the whole of the value it creates. No firm can do this, because willingness to pay is private information, and a customer asked to reveal it has every reason to understate it. Most observed pricing is an attempt to work around that problem.

The crudest method uses an observable characteristic that correlates with willingness to pay — a student discount, a lower fare for older passengers. It is administratively simple and fails whenever the characteristic is a poor proxy or can be borrowed.

The more interesting method makes customers sort themselves. A firm offers versions differing in some attribute, and prices them so that customers reveal their type by choosing. Airlines sell a cheaper ticket that cannot be changed; software is sold in a limited edition alongside a full one. The design constraint is that the cheaper version must be unattractive to high-value customers, which sometimes leads firms to make a product deliberately worse — removing a feature the firm has already built, at some expense, so that the cheap version does not cannibalise the expensive one.

Whether this is good for buyers depends on the alternative. If a single price would have been set high, the availability of a degraded cheap version brings in customers who would otherwise have bought nothing, and they gain. If a single price would have been low, the sorting mainly transfers surplus to the firm. The practice is therefore neither straightforwardly exploitative nor straightforwardly benign, and general claims in either direction usually smuggle in an assumption about which counterfactual applies.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a firm cannot charge each customer that customer's maximum willingness to pay because
options: A. competition law forbids it
B. willingness to pay is private information and customers have reason to understate it
C. customers do not know their own willingness to pay
D. the administrative cost would exceed the gain
E. such prices would be unstable over time
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph. D is a real consideration in practice but not the reason the passage gives.

options: A. exploitative in most circumstances
B. beneficial to buyers in most circumstances
C. impossible to evaluate because the necessary data are private
D. neither, since the answer depends on what single price would otherwise have been set
E. acceptable only where a cheaper version is genuinely inferior

questions.passageTitle: Ulcers and the Weight of Evidence
questions.passageText:
Until the 1980s, peptic ulcers were attributed to stress and excess acid, and treated with acid suppression. The finding that most are associated with a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, and can be cured with antibiotics, is often told as a story of a stubborn establishment refusing an obvious truth. The real sequence is more interesting and less flattering to everybody.

The bacterium had been observed in the stomach lining repeatedly since the nineteenth century, and each time the observation was set aside, partly because it was assumed no organism could survive in gastric acid and partly because contamination was a plausible explanation. When Warren and Marshall proposed the causal link, they had an association and no mechanism, and association with a lesion is weak evidence — the organism could as easily have colonised damaged tissue as caused the damage.

What settled it was a sequence of harder tests: culture of the organism, demonstration that it neutralises acid in its immediate vicinity, self-experimentation producing gastritis, and, decisively, randomised trials showing that eradication cured ulcers and prevented recurrence in a way acid suppression did not.

The episode is cited to argue that medicine resists new ideas, and it did. But the demand for more than an association was not obstinacy; it was the correct response to the evidence then available. What deserves criticism is the earlier century of dismissed observations, when a puzzling finding was repeatedly explained away rather than pursued.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that observations of bacteria in the stomach lining before the 1980s were set aside partly because
options: A. it was assumed no organism could survive gastric acid, and contamination was a plausible explanation
B. the observations could not be reproduced
C. the instruments available were unreliable
D. no treatment existed that could have been tested
E. the observers were not physicians
questions.explanation: Both reasons are given explicitly in the second paragraph.

options: A. Culture of the organism from stomach tissue
B. Self-experimentation producing gastritis

questions.passageText:
Graduates earn more than non-graduates, and the size of the gap is not seriously disputed. Its interpretation is. On the human capital account, education makes people more productive, and the wage difference reflects that added productivity. On the signalling account, education certifies qualities the student already possessed — ability, persistence, tolerance for tedium — which employers cannot observe directly and are willing to pay for.

Distinguishing them is difficult because both predict the same correlation. Several observations bear on the question without settling it. The return to completing a final year is disproportionately large compared with the return to the years before it, which is easier to explain if the certificate matters than if the learning does. Against that, studies exploiting changes in compulsory schooling laws find earnings gains for students who stayed longer without obtaining any additional credential, which signalling alone does not predict.

The shares are what matter for policy, and they differ by field. Where training is specific and demonstrably applied afterwards, the human capital component is likely to dominate. Where a degree functions chiefly as a filter for occupations whose content it never taught, the signalling component is larger, and expanding provision then produces credential inflation rather than productivity: the same jobs come to require higher qualifications, and the private return persists while the social return falls.

The awkwardness of this conclusion is that the two accounts justify very different subsidies while being nearly indistinguishable in the individual case.
questions.prompt: The signalling account holds that education
options: A. makes students more productive in ways employers can observe
B. is valuable mainly for its social connections
C. has no effect on earnings
D. should be provided by employers rather than schools
E. certifies qualities students already possess that employers cannot observe directly
questions.explanation: The definition given in the first paragraph. D misstates it: signalling predicts a wage gap, it simply attributes it differently.

options: A. The return to a final year is disproportionately large.
B. Graduates earn more than non-graduates.
C. The wage gap differs by field of study.
D. Earnings gains appear for students who stayed longer under compulsory schooling laws without gaining a credential.
E. Employers cannot observe persistence directly.
questions.explanation: Extra schooling with no additional certificate produces no additional signal, so a gain there points to something learned. A is the observation that favours signalling.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, credential inflation is most likely where
options: A. training is specific and applied in later work
B. a degree functions chiefly as a filter for occupations whose content it never taught
C. employers can observe ability directly
D. the private return to education is falling
E. compulsory schooling laws are frequently revised
questions.explanation: In that case expanding provision raises the qualifications required for the same jobs, so the private return persists while the social return falls.

questions.passageText:
Many nineteenth-century novels first appeared in monthly or weekly parts, and the arrangement shaped them in ways that are legible in the finished books. Serial publication lowered the price of entry for readers, spreading the cost of a long novel across a year, and it changed what an author could know while writing.

Because early instalments were in print before later ones were drafted, an author received evidence about which characters and situations held an audience, and could respond to it. This is usually described as a compromise of artistic integrity. It is better understood as a different compositional situation: the writer worked with feedback, as a dramatist does, rather than in the closed conditions the later novel took as standard.

The form imposed its own requirements. Each part needed a shape of its own and a reason to buy the next one, which encouraged the recurring cliffhanger and a density of incident that later critics, reading the parts bound together, mistook for undisciplined excess. It also encouraged large casts, since a novel appearing over eighteen months must reintroduce its people to readers who last met them weeks earlier — hence the repeated identifying tags that read as mannerism on the page but functioned as memory aids.

Recovering this makes certain criticisms harder to sustain. A structure that seems padded when read in a week may be well proportioned when read across a year, and judging a serial novel by the conventions of a book conceived whole is a category error rather than a discovery about its quality.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that an author writing in instalments
options: A. received evidence about audience response while the novel was still being written
B. had less control over the plot than a dramatist
C. was required to submit the complete manuscript in advance
D. wrote more slowly than authors publishing whole volumes
E. could not revise earlier instalments
questions.explanation: That feedback is the compositional difference the passage builds on. E is true incidentally but is not what the passage highlights as the author's situation.

options: A. a useful corrective to nineteenth-century excess

readingPassages.title: What a Degree Signals
readingPassages.text:
Graduates earn more than non-graduates, and the size of the gap is not seriously disputed. Its interpretation is. On the human capital account, education makes people more productive, and the wage difference reflects that added productivity. On the signalling account, education certifies qualities the student already possessed — ability, persistence, tolerance for tedium — which employers cannot observe directly and are willing to pay for.

Distinguishing them is difficult because both predict the same correlation. Several observations bear on the question without settling it. The return to completing a final year is disproportionately large compared with the return to the years before it, which is easier to explain if the certificate matters than if the learning does. Against that, studies exploiting changes in compulsory schooling laws find earnings gains for students who stayed longer without obtaining any additional credential, which signalling alone does not predict.

The shares are what matter for policy, and they differ by field. Where training is specific and demonstrably applied afterwards, the human capital component is likely to dominate. Where a degree functions chiefly as a filter for occupations whose content it never taught, the signalling component is larger, and expanding provision then produces credential inflation rather than productivity: the same jobs come to require higher qualifications, and the private return persists while the social return falls.

The awkwardness of this conclusion is that the two accounts justify very different subsidies while being nearly indistinguishable in the individual case.

readingPassages.title: Fiction in Instalments
readingPassages.text:
Many nineteenth-century novels first appeared in monthly or weekly parts, and the arrangement shaped them in ways that are legible in the finished books. Serial publication lowered the price of entry for readers, spreading the cost of a long novel across a year, and it changed what an author could know while writing.

Because early instalments were in print before later ones were drafted, an author received evidence about which characters and situations held an audience, and could respond to it. This is usually described as a compromise of artistic integrity. It is better understood as a different compositional situation: the writer worked with feedback, as a dramatist does, rather than in the closed conditions the later novel took as standard.

The form imposed its own requirements. Each part needed a shape of its own and a reason to buy the next one, which encouraged the recurring cliffhanger and a density of incident that later critics, reading the parts bound together, mistook for undisciplined excess. It also encouraged large casts, since a novel appearing over eighteen months must reintroduce its people to readers who last met them weeks earlier — hence the repeated identifying tags that read as mannerism on the page but functioned as memory aids.

Recovering this makes certain criticisms harder to sustain. A structure that seems padded when read in a week may be well proportioned when read across a year, and judging a serial novel by the conventions of a book conceived whole is a category error rather than a discovery about its quality.
